$comment: CLADES rule library. Every threshold, weight and explanation lives here. Rules can be added (formula language: see src/rules/formula.ts), tuned or disabled ('enabled': false) without code changes. Weights and amber/red cut-offs are the author's judgment, NOT calibrated on Indian data; the back-test (build 8) exists to challenge them.

beneish.$comment: Beneish (1999), 'The Detection of Earnings Manipulation', Financial Analysts Journal 55(5). Reference means below: verify against the paper; US sample; recalibrate on Indian data.

DSRI.name: Days sales in receivables index
DSRI.plain: Customers owe a bigger share of sales than last year. Sales may have been booked before the cash was certain.
DSRI.innocent: Longer credit terms to win customers, or a large order shipped just before year-end.
DSRI.nextStep: Read the receivables ageing note: how much is older than six months, and how much is from related parties?

GMI.name: Gross margin index
GMI.plain: Gross margin fell. Companies with worsening margins are under more pressure to make the numbers look better.
GMI.innocent: Raw-material price spike, a change in product mix, or deliberate price cuts.
GMI.nextStep: Compare the margin fall with listed peers and with input-cost movements in the same year.

AQI.name: Asset quality index
AQI.plain: A larger share of assets is neither current assets nor plant. Costs may be parked on the balance sheet instead of being expensed.
AQI.innocent: An acquisition (goodwill), new long-term investments, or a genuine capital project under construction.
AQI.nextStep: Find what grew in non-current assets: capital work-in-progress, intangibles, investments or 'other' assets.

SGI.name: Sales growth index
SGI.plain: Sales grew fast. Growth is not a problem in itself, but fast growers face pressure to keep the streak alive.
SGI.innocent: Real demand, new capacity, an acquisition or a low base.
SGI.nextStep: Check whether cash collected from customers grew in line with reported sales.

DEPI.name: Depreciation index
DEPI.plain: Assets are being depreciated more slowly than last year, which lifts reported profit.
DEPI.innocent: Large new assets added late in the year, or a documented reassessment of useful lives.
DEPI.nextStep: Read the accounting-policy note for any change in useful lives or depreciation method.

SGAI.name: SG&A index
SGAI.plain: Shown for completeness only. In Beneish's own sample this ratio barely differed between the two groups and its weight in the model is negative, so it is not traffic-lighted.
SGAI.innocent: Not applicable: this ratio has weak discriminating power.

TATA.name: Total accruals to total assets
TATA.plain: Profit is running ahead of cash. The gap is made of accounting estimates rather than money received.
TATA.innocent: A working-capital build for real growth, or a one-off timing difference around year-end.
TATA.nextStep: Reconcile profit to operating cash flow line by line and see which working-capital item absorbed the cash.

LVGI.name: Leverage index
LVGI.plain: Leverage rose. More debt means tighter covenants and more pressure. Note: its weight in the M-score is negative and was not statistically significant in the paper.
LVGI.innocent: Debt-funded expansion that has not started earning yet.
LVGI.nextStep: Check debt covenants and the repayment schedule in the borrowings note.

combos.text: Profit not backed by cash, receivables outrunning sales and an elevated M-score appear together. Each is weak alone; together they are a classic early pattern.
Eight or more checks are at amber or worse. Several weak signals together deserve more attention than any one of them.
Two independent models flag this company.
Three or more independent models flag this company.

honestProfit.$comment: Default stress-test assumptions. Every one is adjustable with a slider on the dashboard. They are deliberately harsh round numbers, not estimates of what is true.

rules.title: Beneish M-score
rules.plain: The eight Beneish ratios combined. Above -1.78, the accounts resemble those of companies that later restated earnings (in a 1980s-90s US sample).
rules.innocent: Fast-growing, acquisitive or working-capital-heavy companies often score high for honest reasons.
rules.nextStep: Open the Beneish tab and see which of the eight ratios drive the score.

rules.title: Accruals ratio (Sloan)
rules.plain: The part of profit that did not arrive as cash, as a share of average assets. High-accrual profits have historically reversed more often.
rules.innocent: Working capital built up to support real growth.
rules.nextStep: Check whether the accrual build reverses in the next two half-year results.

rules.title: Profit not backed by cash (CFO / PAT)
rules.plain: For every rupee of reported profit, this many rupees of cash came in from operations.
rules.innocent: One-off working-capital build, or advance tax and inventory stocking before a launch.
rules.nextStep: Ask why cash from operations lagged profit this year and whether it has caught up since.

rules.title: Cumulative CFO / PAT (3 to 5 years)
rules.plain: Over several years timing differences should wash out. Profit that never turns into cash over three to five years is the harder kind to explain.
rules.innocent: A long project cycle or sustained fast growth can hold cash conversion down for years.
rules.nextStep: Add up five years of profit and five years of operating cash flow from the annual reports and compare.

rules.title: Receivables outpace sales
rules.plain: Receivables grew this many percentage points faster than sales.
rules.innocent: A large year-end order, a new customer segment with longer credit, or export growth.
rules.nextStep: Look for the split of receivables by age and by related vs unrelated customers.

rules.title: Days sales outstanding rising
rules.plain: Customers are taking this many more days to pay than a year ago.
rules.innocent: Change in customer mix or deliberate credit extension.
rules.nextStep: Compare DSO with two or three listed peers.

rules.title: Growth far above sector
rules.plain: Sales growth exceeds the sector reference by this many percentage points.
rules.innocent: Market-share gains, new capacity or an acquisition.
rules.nextStep: Check whether volumes, capacity and headcount grew consistently with the sales claimed.

rules.title: Capex vs depreciation
rules.plain: Capital spending is this many times depreciation. Very high multiples can hide operating costs recorded as assets.
rules.innocent: A genuine expansion phase.
rules.nextStep: Match capex to commissioned capacity announced by the company.

rules.title: Capital work-in-progress share
rules.plain: This share of fixed assets is still 'under construction' and is not being depreciated.
rules.innocent: A large plant genuinely being built.
rules.nextStep: Read the CWIP ageing schedule (mandatory under Schedule III) for projects overdue or suspended.

rules.title: CWIP stuck for 3+ years (floor estimate)
rules.plain: At least this share of fixed assets has sat in work-in-progress in each of the last four balance sheets. Projects may have rotated, so this is an estimate from totals, not from the ageing note.
rules.innocent: Rolling multi-year projects where old ones finish as new ones start.
rules.nextStep: Use the CWIP ageing note to confirm how much is really older than three years.

rules.title: Intangibles growing faster than sales
rules.plain: Intangible assets grew this many percentage points faster than sales. Capitalised development or software costs lift profit today.
rules.innocent: An acquisition or a real product-development programme.
rules.nextStep: Check the intangibles note for 'internally generated' additions.

rules.title: Cash-rich yet borrowing
rules.plain: The company holds large cash and large debt at once (the smaller of the two is this share of assets). Paying interest while sitting on cash needs a reason.
rules.innocent: Cash held in subsidiaries or overseas, earmarked for capex, or restricted as margin money.
rules.nextStep: Check how much of the cash is 'other bank balances', pledged or held by subsidiaries.

rules.title: Return earned on cash and investments
rules.formula: when((cash + investments) / totalAssets > 0.1, otherIncome / avg(cash + investments, lag(cash + investments, 1)))
rules.plain: Other income as a return on average cash and investments. A very low return on a large balance raises the question of whether the balance was there all year.
rules.innocent: Balances built up only at year-end, or held in non-interest current accounts or strategic equity stakes.
rules.nextStep: Compare interest income in the notes with average month-end balances if disclosed.

rules.title: Debt rising while profit rises
rules.plain: Borrowings grew this much in a year when profit also grew. Profitable companies that keep borrowing may not be generating the cash they report.
rules.innocent: Debt-funded capacity expansion.
rules.nextStep: See what the new borrowing funded: capex, working capital or loans to group companies.

rules.title: Interest coverage
rules.plain: Operating profit covers the interest bill this many times.
rules.innocent: A temporary dip in a cyclical business.
rules.nextStep: Check upcoming repayments and any covenant waivers mentioned in the notes.

rules.battery: E Too good to be true
rules.title: Unusually smooth margins
rules.plain: Operating margin moved by only this much (standard deviation) over four to five years. Real businesses wobble.
rules.innocent: Regulated returns, long-term contracts or a dominant brand with pricing power.
rules.nextStep: Compare margin stability with the closest listed peers.

rules.battery: E Too good to be true
rules.title: Return on equity far above sector
rules.formula: when(avg(equity, lag(equity, 1)) > 0, netIncome / avg(equity, lag(equity, 1)) - bench("roe"))
rules.plain: Return on equity exceeds the sector reference by this many percentage points.
rules.innocent: A real competitive advantage, an asset-light model or high payout shrinking equity.
rules.nextStep: Identify what protects the excess return and whether peers confirm it.

rules.battery: E Too good to be true
rules.title: Benford first-digit test (chi-square)
rules.plain: First digits of the reported figures compared with Benford's law (chi-square, 8 degrees of freedom; 15.51 = 5% level, 20.09 = 1% level). NOT SCORED (weight 0): a company's line items over several years are strongly correlated, which breaks the test's independence assumption. On CLADES's own synthetic clean company it raised a false alarm, so it is shown for information only.
rules.innocent: Small samples and related line items routinely deviate from Benford's law.
rules.nextStep: Treat as a tie-breaker only; never act on this test alone.

rules.title: Cash flow vs balance-sheet cash
rules.plain: Net cash flow differs from the change in balance-sheet cash by this share of assets.
rules.innocent: The balance sheet line often includes bank deposits that the cash flow statement excludes.
rules.nextStep: Reconcile cash and cash equivalents using the note to the cash flow statement.

rules.title: Effective tax rate
rules.plain: Tax charged as a share of pre-tax profit. Profit that the tax authorities are not asked to tax deserves a look.
rules.innocent: SEZ or other tax holidays, brought-forward losses, MAT credit or deferred-tax adjustments.
rules.nextStep: Read the tax reconciliation note and compare tax paid in the cash flow statement.

rules.title: Dividends covered by operating cash
rules.plain: Operating cash flow covers the dividend this many times. Below 1, dividends were funded from borrowings or reserves of cash.
rules.innocent: A special dividend, or a temporary cash-flow dip in a company with ample cash.
rules.nextStep: Check whether borrowings rose in the year the dividend was paid.

rules.title: Implied interest rate on debt
rules.formula: when(avg(borrowings, lag(borrowings, 1)) / totalAssets > 0.1, interest / avg(borrowings, lag(borrowings, 1)))
rules.plain: Interest expense as a rate on average debt. A rate far below market suggests interest is being capitalised into assets rather than expensed.
rules.innocent: Low-cost foreign-currency loans, interest-free group loans, or debt drawn late in the year.
rules.nextStep: Find 'borrowing costs capitalised' in the PPE or finance-cost note.

rules.title: Other income share of profit
rules.plain: This share of pre-tax profit comes from 'other income' rather than the business itself.
rules.innocent: A cash-rich company earning treasury income, or a one-off asset sale.
rules.nextStep: Break other income into interest, gains on sale and anything described as 'miscellaneous'.

rules.title: Promoter shares pledged
rules.plain: This percentage of the promoters' holding is pledged to lenders. A falling share price can then force the promoters' hand.
rules.innocent: Pledges backing loans for the company's own expansion.
rules.nextStep: Check the latest shareholding pattern filing for the trend in pledged shares.

rules.title: Loans and advances to promoter entities
rules.plain: Loans and advances to related parties equal this share of net worth. Money can leave a listed company this way.
rules.innocent: Funding of a subsidiary's genuine project on arm's-length terms.
rules.nextStep: Read the related-party note: who received the money, on what terms, and has any been repaid?

rules.title: Contingent liabilities vs net worth
rules.plain: Off-balance-sheet contingent liabilities equal this share of net worth.
rules.innocent: Routine tax disputes and bank guarantees common in the industry.
rules.nextStep: Check for corporate guarantees given for group companies' loans.

rules.title: Altman Z'' (emerging markets)
rules.plain: A distress score. Below 4.15 is the distress zone, above 5.85 the safe zone. Companies in distress have the strongest motive to flatter results.
rules.innocent: Capital-intensive businesses in an investment phase can sit in the grey zone for years.
rules.nextStep: Check liquidity: cash, undrawn credit lines and debt due within a year.

rules.title: Piotroski F-score
rules.plain: Nine simple pass/fail tests of profitability, leverage and efficiency. Three or fewer is weak.
rules.innocent: One bad year in a cyclical business drags several of the nine tests at once.
rules.nextStep: See which of the nine tests failed and whether they share one cause.
